items.prompt: What is the main purpose of the subject line in a business email?

options.label: To thank the reader in advance for the time spent reading the message
To show the writer's job title and contact details before the message
To tell the reader what the message covers so they can prioritise it
To repeat the whole message so that readers can skip the body entirely

rubric: The subject line signals topic and priority so the reader can decide how to handle the email.
Distractors confuse it with a summary, a signature or a courtesy line.

items.prompt: In the direct approach to business writing, where does the main point or request normally go?

options.label: At the start
After all background
In the closing line
In the signature block

rubric: The direct approach states the main point first, then gives support.
Distractors reflect the habit of building up to the point, which is the indirect approach.

items.prompt: Which set of headings normally appears at the top of a business memo?

options.label: Dear, Yours, Regards, PS
To, From, Date, Subject
Header, Footer, Margin, Page
Title, Author, Index, Abstract

rubric: A memo header lists To, From, Date and Subject.
Other options come from letters, academic papers or page layout.

items.prompt: What is the name of the short section at the start of a report that summarises its key findings and recommendations for busy readers?

options.label: Table of contents
Reference list
Executive summary
Appendix

rubric: The executive summary condenses findings and recommendations at the front of a report.
The other terms name back-matter sections with different purposes.

items.prompt: Which grammatical voice is generally preferred in clear, concise business writing?

options.label: Passive voice
Conditional mood
Active voice
Future perfect tense

rubric: Active voice names who does what and is usually shorter and clearer.
Passive voice is a common but weaker habit; the others are not voices.

items.prompt: Which of the following are standard parts of a business proposal? Select all that apply.

options.label: Costs or budget
Proposed solution and timeline
Personal anecdotes about the writer's weekend
Executive summary
Decorative emojis in the heading

rubric: Proposals typically include a summary, the solution with timeline, and costs.
Personal anecdotes and emojis have no place in a standard proposal.

items.prompt: Priya must email her manager to get a purchase approved before Friday's order deadline. She has already written the background and the costs. Which element must she include so the manager knows exactly what to do?

options.label: A clear request for approval that states the Friday deadline
A comparison of the suppliers the team has used in recent years
A friendly opening line so that the email feels less formal to read
A fuller history of how the current supplier was originally chosen

rubric: A clear call to action with a deadline tells the reader what is needed and by when.
Distractors add background or tone but leave the action unclear.

items.prompt: Why does a business email to a busy executive usually state the request in the first lines?

options.label: Readers decide quickly what to do and may stop after the opening
Grammar rules require the main clause to appear at the very top
Executives read only the first sentence of any email, whatever it says
Long background first makes a request seem more polite and persuasive

rubric: Putting the request first respects limited reader time and makes action easy.
Distractors misjudge politeness, reader behaviour or grammar as the reason.

items.prompt: Which rewrite of 'Due to the fact that the server was down, we were unable to process your order' is the most concise while keeping the meaning?

options.label: Because the server was down, we could not process your order.
The server being down was the reason we were unable to process it.
We were unable to process your order, due to the fact of the server.
Due to the server's downtime, processing of your order was not possible.

rubric: 'Because' replaces the wordy phrase and the active verb keeps it short.
Other options keep wordy or passive constructions.

items.prompt: Which sentence has the most appropriate tone for a first email to a new client?

options.label: As I mentioned in my earlier message, which you may have missed, our price list is attached again.
Thank you for your enquiry; I have attached our price list for your review.
It's great to finally hear from you, as we expected your enquiry weeks ago. Our price list is attached.
Hey! Here's our price list, let me know what u think whenever you get a sec.

rubric: A polite, courteous and neutral tone suits a first professional contact.
Distractors are too casual, impatient or accusatory.

items.prompt: What does the principle 'bottom line up front' (BLUF) mean when writing a message?

options.label: Open with the budget figures before any other content
Lead with the conclusion or request, then add supporting detail
Give all the evidence first and state the conclusion at the end
Close the message with a recap of the earlier background

rubric: BLUF puts the conclusion or request first and the support after it.
Distractors confuse it with financial content or with building up to a conclusion.

items.prompt: A report goes to senior executives, not to the technical team. Why should it use a short summary and plain language?

options.label: They have limited time and need to decide, not follow the methods
Executives prefer reports that leave out recommendations
They cannot understand any technical idea however well it is explained
Plain language makes a report look shorter than its real length

rubric: Writing for the audience means giving decision-makers what they need quickly.
Distractors assume wrongly that executives lack ability or want less content.

items.prompt: Which edits would make a draft more concise without changing its meaning? Select all that apply.

options.label: Delete a sentence that repeats the previous one
Replace 'at this point in time' with 'now'
Add a paragraph of background to each point
Add extra adjectives to every noun
Replace 'in order to' with 'to'

rubric: Cutting wordy phrases and repetition shortens text while keeping meaning.
Adding adjectives or background makes the text longer, not more concise.

items.prompt: A team lead emails colleagues in three time zones: 'Please send me the figures ASAP.' Replies arrive over three days, and several people say they were unsure how urgent it was. What is the best explanation and fix?

options.label: A written request is too blunt without a deadline; ask for the figures 'when convenient' to stay polite
ASAP means different things to different readers; give a date and time
The email is too short to convey urgency; add several sentences explaining why the figures matter
ASAP is too formal for colleagues in other offices; use 'whenever you can' so replies feel relaxed

rubric: Vague urgency terms are read differently; a specific date and time removes doubt.
Distractors misdiagnose the problem as formality, length or the presence of deadlines.

items.prompt: Which subject line best tells the reader what the email is about and what is needed?

options.label: Quick question about something important for us
Approval needed by Friday: Q3 training budget
Following up on our conversation from last week's meeting
Update on the project situation as of today

rubric: It states the action and the deadline, so the reader knows what to do.
The others are vague and could describe any email.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of an executive summary at the start of a report?

options.label: It introduces the author and explains why the report was originally commissioned
It records every data source and method so readers can repeat the study exactly
It lets decision-makers see the findings and recommendation without reading it all
It previews each section in order so readers can skip ahead to the details

rubric: A summary serves busy decision-makers who may read nothing else.
Distractors confuse it with a methods section, an introduction or a table of contents.

items.prompt: Why is active voice usually preferred in business writing?

options.label: It lets the writer leave out the subject so the tone stays neutral
It makes sentences longer, which signals thoroughness to the reader
It names who is doing what, so actions and responsibility are clear
It always sounds more formal, which readers expect in business writing

rubric: Active voice makes the actor and the action explicit.
Distractors mistake formality, length or vagueness for good style.

items.prompt: Which sentence strikes the right tone for a first email to a client about a late delivery?

options.label: Hi! Sorry about that, stuff happens with suppliers, so it should show up soon.
Sorry, your order will arrive Thursday, two days late. Tracking will be emailed today.
Unfortunately, it has come to our attention that certain delays have occurred in delivery.
Your order is late because of supplier problems, and we cannot change that.

rubric: It apologises briefly, is specific and tells the client what happens next, in a polite and direct tone.
The others are defensive, evasive and stiff, or too casual and vague.

items.prompt: A writer puts three separate requests in the middle of one long paragraph of an email. What is the most likely result?

options.label: The reader replies to one request and overlooks the others
The reader answers every request because long emails seem urgent
The reader waits for a reminder before reading it at all
The reader forwards it to a manager to decide which to answer

rubric: Requests buried in dense text are easily missed; readers skim.
Distractors assume length creates urgency or that readers behave in unrealistic ways.

items.prompt: Which edits make a sentence more concise without changing its meaning? Select all that apply.

options.label: Change 'in the event that' to 'if'
Change 'due to the fact that' to 'because'
Add 'basically' before each main point
Restate each point in different words at the end

rubric: Both replacements swap wordy phrases for single words with the same meaning.
Adding filler or repeating points makes writing longer, not tighter.

items.prompt: A manager receives an email from a colleague. It opens with three paragraphs of project history, and only the last line asks, 'Can you approve the extra budget by Thursday?' The manager nearly missed it. What is the main weakness in how the email is organised?

options.label: The email includes project history, which should never appear in workplace messages
The deadline is stated, which makes the request sound pushy to senior readers
The action is buried at the end, behind background the reader does not need first
The greeting is too informal, so the reader does not take the request seriously

rubric: The ask should come first, with only the background needed to support it.
Distractors blame tone, banned content or stating a deadline, none of which is the real issue.

items.prompt: You need your manager to approve a $2,000 software renewal by Friday. Which opening line for your email works best?

options.label: Please approve the $2,000 software renewal by Friday so our licence does not lapse.
I wanted to touch base about some thoughts I have had regarding our software tools.
I hope you are well. As you know, we have used this software since 2021 and it has helped.
Our software licence is up for renewal, and there are several options to consider here.

rubric: It puts the request, amount, deadline and reason up front.
Distractors delay or blur the ask with pleasantries, vagueness or background.

items.prompt: You are writing a memo announcing that the staff car park closes for repairs from 3 June. Which structure puts the content in the best order?

options.label: Greeting, apology for inconvenience, details of the contractor, dates in the final paragraph
Subject reading 'Notice', long explanation of repairs, then alternatives, then dates
Subject naming the closure, dates, what staff should do instead, who to contact
History of the car park, reasons for repairs, closure dates, a thank-you for patience

rubric: A memo leads with the what and when, then the action required and a contact.
Distractors bury the dates or open with unneeded background.

items.prompt: A colleague has missed a deadline for figures you need. Which message is best to send?

options.label: No worries about the deadline at all, just send the figures over whenever you get a free chance.
You missed the deadline again, so please send the figures tomorrow and make sure it is not late this time.
Per my previous email, the figures are overdue and must be sent to me immediately without any more delay.
Could you send the figures by noon tomorrow? I need time to check them before the 2 pm client call.

rubric: It is polite, gives a specific time and a reason.
Distractors are accusatory, passive-aggressive or give no deadline.

items.prompt: You must explain four steps for submitting an expense claim, in order, to new staff. Which format suits best?

options.label: A table with a column for who owns each step
A single paragraph that covers all four steps
A numbered list, each step starting with a verb
A bulleted list ordered by how important each step is

rubric: Sequential steps suit a numbered list with action verbs.
Paragraphs, importance-ordered bullets or tables hide or disrupt the order.

items.prompt: You are ending an email that sends a proposal to a client and you need a decision. Which closing line is best?

options.label: Please confirm by 5 May if you would like to proceed, and I will book the start date.
I look forward to hearing from you in due course regarding the proposal and its terms.
Let me know your thoughts whenever it is convenient, and we can discuss next steps then.
Feel free to reach out if you have any questions, concerns or suggestions at any point.

rubric: It names the action, a deadline and what happens next.
Distractors are open-ended and give the reader no date or clear step.

items.prompt: Edit this sentence: 'The meeting that is scheduled for Tuesday has been postponed by management until such time as a new date is able to be confirmed.' Which edits improve it? Select all that apply.

options.label: Replace 'until such time as' with 'until'
Move 'Tuesday' to the end of the sentence
Use active voice: 'Management has postponed Tuesday's meeting'
Add 'very much' before 'postponed' for emphasis

rubric: Active voice and a shorter connector cut words and clarify the actor.
Adding emphasis or moving words does not improve clarity.

items.prompt: A customer emails that she was charged twice for one order. You have confirmed the error, and a $45 refund will reach her account in 3 to 5 days. Which reply plan is best?

options.label: Apologise briefly, say the $45 refund arrives in 3 to 5 days, and give a contact for follow-up
Ask her to resend the order details, then confirm the refund once you have rechecked them
Explain how the billing system works, then mention the refund near the end of the email
Quote the policy on duplicate charges, then offer the refund as a one-time goodwill gesture

rubric: It apologises, gives the solution with specifics and offers a next contact.
Distractors delay the fix, add unneeded checks or frame a mistake as a favour.

items.prompt: You need a director to approve a $12,000 training budget by Friday. Which opening sentence best applies the bottom-line-up-front approach?

options.label: Over the past quarter, our team has noticed several skill gaps that training could help to address.
Attached is a document that contains details about training costs, vendors and possible start dates.
I hope your week is going well, and I wanted to share some background on our team's training needs.
Please approve the $12,000 training budget by Friday so the course can start on time.

rubric: The key opens with the decision, amount and deadline so the reader knows the ask immediately.
Distractors open with pleasantries, background or an attachment, which delay the request.

items.prompt: Which rewrite of this sentence is clearest and most concise? 'We are in receipt of your request and will make a determination regarding approval by Friday.'

options.label: Your request is received; approval will be determined by us by the Friday of this week.
We received your request and will decide by Friday.
Your request has been received, and a determination will be made on approval by Friday.
We have received your request and are currently in the process of deciding on it by Friday.

rubric: The key uses active verbs and plain words, replacing the nominalisation 'make a determination' with 'decide'.
Distractors keep passive or wordy structures that sound formal but add no meaning.

items.prompt: You are emailing 30 staff to submit timesheets by 5 pm this Thursday. Which subject line works best?

options.label: Timesheet policy update: please read the attached submission process before the end of the week
Reminder from Payroll about the timesheet cutoff and what happens when entries arrive late
Action needed: submit timesheets by 5 pm Thursday
Timesheets, please: payroll runs soon and we need everyone's hours entered correctly

rubric: The key states the action and deadline, so readers can act even without opening the email.
Distractors are vague, omit the deadline or signal information rather than a required action.

items.prompt: You are writing a memo to executives recommending a switch of software vendor. Which section order best fits their need to make a decision?

options.label: Cost tables first, then methodology, then a short note about what we suggest
Greeting, company history with vendors, a list of all features, then a closing thanks
Background history, vendor comparison details, analysis, and finally the recommendation to switch
Recommendation, key reasons, cost and risk, then next steps requested

rubric: Executives need the conclusion first, then support, then the action required of them.
Distractors bury the recommendation after background or data, the chronological or data-first habit.

items.prompt: A client asks for a 10% discount you cannot give. Which sentence declines while keeping the relationship and giving a clear answer?

options.label: We would love to help but it's simply impossible, so please accept our price as it stands.
Unfortunately, our policy does not allow discounts, and we cannot make any exceptions to it.
We can't offer a discount, but we can add two free training sessions at the quoted price.
Your request is noted; however, discounts are under review and may be considered in future.

rubric: The key is clear about the refusal and offers an alternative that serves the client's interest.
Distractors are curt, blame-leaning, or falsely imply the discount might still happen.

items.prompt: A 220-word client email has a long greeting paragraph, repeated points, and three separate requests in one paragraph. Which edits apply concise, action-oriented writing? Select all that apply.

options.label: Split the three requests into a short numbered list
Add a closing paragraph that summarises the whole email again
Replace the opening with a one-line statement of purpose
Cut the repeated points so each is stated once
Turn all sentences into passive voice to sound formal

rubric: Removing repetition, listing requests and stating purpose upfront all shorten the email and make actions easy to find.
Re-summarising adds length and passive voice reduces clarity.

items.prompt: A project sponsor reads email on her phone between meetings. You must tell her a launch is delayed two weeks by a supplier fault, and she must decide by noon whether to approve $4,000 in overtime. How should you format the message?

options.label: Use a long, apologetic opening to soften the news, then list every timeline change in one dense paragraph
Subject says a decision is needed by noon; first line gives the delay and the ask; two short bullets cover cause and cost
Attach a detailed report, and write only 'See attached for the update' in the body to keep it short
Neutral subject; start with the supplier's history, then explain the fault, and put the overtime request in the last paragraph

rubric: The key puts the decision and deadline where a mobile skimmer sees them first, with brief support.
Distractors bury the ask, hide it in an attachment, or overload a small screen.

items.prompt: A manager emails a team with three paragraphs of background, then 'Please send me your figures' in paragraph four. Half the team never replies. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The tone was too polite and indirect, which made the request seem optional to most of the team
The background paragraphs were too brief to persuade readers that the figures task really mattered
The word 'please' signals low priority, so readers postponed the request until a later date
The request sits after three paragraphs of background, so skimmers miss the action and deadline

rubric: Burying the ask means skimming readers never reach it; structure, not politeness, is the fault.
Distractors blame tone or word choice, which do not explain why the request went unseen.

items.prompt: A 20-page report's executive summary reads: 'This report examines customer churn. Section 1 covers methods, Section 2 covers data...' Executives say it doesn't help them decide. What is the underlying flaw?

options.label: It is written in the present tense, which makes the findings seem less certain to executive readers
It describes the report's contents rather than stating findings, conclusions and the decisions recommended
It gives too little technical detail about methods, which executives need before they will trust findings
It is too short to represent twenty pages fairly, so it needs a full paragraph for every section

rubric: A summary must carry the findings and recommendations, not a table of contents in prose.
Distractors focus on length, tense or method detail, which are not what executives need to decide.

items.prompt: A proposal details the vendor's 15 product features. The client's stated concern was cutting order-processing time, and it says it 'didn't see the fit.' What best explains the failure?

options.label: The proposal lacked urgent language, so the client felt no pressure to move quickly towards a decision
The detail was fine, but the proposal lacked a formal cover page and table of contents for navigation
The content was organised around the vendor's offering instead of the client's stated problem and outcome
Fifteen features is simply too many, so trimming the list to ten would have made the proposal persuasive

rubric: Persuasive proposals tie the solution to the reader's stated problem and benefit.
Distractors treat feature count, urgency or formatting as the cause, missing the audience mismatch.

items.prompt: A colleague replies to a late file with: 'As per my previous email, I still need the file today.' The recipient becomes defensive. Which analysis best explains this and the fix?

options.label: The phrase implies blame; restating the need and deadline neutrally ('I need the file by 3 pm today') keeps focus on action
'As per' is outdated jargon; swapping in casual slang would make the whole message sound friendlier to read
Referring to the earlier email is fine; adding exclamation marks would restore the warm tone the message lacks
The deadline is too tight; moving it to tomorrow would remove the pressure that triggered the defensive reaction

rubric: 'As per my previous email' signals reproach; a neutral, specific ask removes blame and keeps the deadline.
Distractors misidentify the cause as the deadline, the register or missing punctuation.

items.prompt: A memo to frontline staff about a new refund system uses phrases like 'leverage the workflow' and 'sunset the legacy process.' Staff keep asking basic questions. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: The terms are acceptable for this audience, but the memo should be re-sent weekly to reinforce it
The memo is too short, so adding a page of company background would help staff grasp the new system
Staff are skimming carelessly, so the memo needs bold type applied throughout to force their attention
Abstract jargon hides the concrete steps, so the memo needs plain verbs and one worked refund example

rubric: Abstract wording hides what staff must do; plain verbs and an example make steps concrete.
Distractors blame reader effort, length or frequency rather than the mismatch between wording and audience.

items.prompt: A draft email says: 'We should probably look at the numbers soon and someone could send them over when possible.' Which flaws make it likely to produce no action? Select all that apply.

options.label: Hedging words like 'probably' and 'could' make it sound optional
No deadline or specific time is given
No named owner is assigned to the task
The sentences are too short and direct
The vocabulary is too formal for a workplace email

rubric: Missing owner, missing deadline and hedging each let readers treat the task as someone else's or optional.
Short, direct sentences and formality are not the cause of inaction here.

items.prompt: A 14-message reply-all thread about a client event ends with two people each assuming the other booked the venue. The lead's final message read: 'Great, let's get this sorted by next week.' What is the key flaw in that message?

options.label: It is too brief to show the lead understood the thread's long history of earlier decisions
It assigns no owner or specific deadline, so each reader can assume someone else will act
It was sent to everyone, so it should have gone only to the most senior person on the thread
It sounds too positive, so readers think the problem is solved and stop reading the thread

rubric: Without a named owner and date, responsibility diffuses and the venue stays unbooked.
Distractors blame brevity, audience or tone rather than the missing accountability.

items.prompt: A project lead emails a director: three paragraphs of background, then a last line reading 'Let me know your thoughts when you can.' There is no reply after a week. Which diagnosis best explains the silence?

options.label: The email went to too few people, so the director assumed someone else would take ownership of a reply
The background was too short, so the director lacked the context needed to respond with any confidence
The request is vague and buried at the end, so the director cannot tell what decision is needed or by when
The tone was too polite, so the director read it as optional and gave it low priority against other work

rubric: The ask is unclear, buried and has no deadline, so the reader has no action to take.
Distractors blame tone, context or recipients, when the structural flaw is the missing explicit request.

items.prompt: A memo states: 'It was decided that the vendor list would be reviewed and updates would be submitted by month-end.' Month-end passes with no action. What is the most precise flaw in the sentence?

options.label: Passive constructions hide who must review and who must submit, so no one recognises the task as theirs
The word 'decided' sounds final, so readers assume the work has already been done by someone else
The sentence is too long, so readers lose the thread before reaching the month-end date at the very end
The date is placed last, so readers treat it as a soft suggestion instead of a firm requirement

rubric: Passive voice removes the actor, so responsibility is diffuse.
Other options point to length, position or word choice, which do not explain why nobody acted.

items.prompt: A report summary opens: 'We surveyed 400 customers over six weeks using a mixed-method approach.' Executives say they still do not know what to do. Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: The summary should be moved to the end, so that the full evidence appears before any conclusions
The summary should give more detail about the sampling and method first, so that executives can trust the results
The summary leads with method, not findings and recommendation, so decision-relevant content is missing
The summary is too formal in register, so executives cannot connect with the people who were surveyed

rubric: Executives need the conclusion and recommendation up front; method belongs in supporting detail.
Distractors add more method or move the summary, which deepens the problem.

items.prompt: An analyst writes: 'I was just wondering if you might possibly be able to look at the invoice when you get a chance, no worries if not.' The invoice stays unpaid. Which analysis is most accurate?

options.label: The greeting is missing, so the reader treats the message as impersonal and does not feel obliged to reply
The message is too short, so the reader assumes it is unimportant compared with longer emails received
The word 'invoice' is too specific, so the reader cannot tell which department should handle the matter
Stacked hedges and an explicit opt-out remove urgency and give the reader an easy exit from acting

rubric: Hedging phrases plus 'no worries if not' signal the task is optional.
Other options blame length, wording or greeting, none of which weakens the ask this much.

items.prompt: A proposal for new scheduling software lists its features in detail. The committee, whose stated criterion was reducing overtime cost, rejects it. What best explains the rejection?

options.label: The feature list was organised by product module, so the committee could not compare it side by side with competing software
The proposal described what the software does but never tied those features to the committee's decision criterion
The proposal relied on dense technical specifications, so the committee found it too hard to read in a single sitting
The proposal's confident, promotional tone made the committee distrust its claims about what the product could deliver

rubric: Proposals persuade when benefits are framed against the reader's decision criteria.
Distractors target feature count, numeric density or tone rather than relevance to the criterion.

items.prompt: An announcement has the subject 'Update', gives the deadline as '3/4' in the fifth paragraph, and goes to staff in several countries. It is written in short paragraphs in a polite, formal tone. Many miss the deadline. Which features plausibly contributed? Select all that apply.

options.label: '3/4' can be read as 3 April or 4 March
The deadline sits in the fifth paragraph, where skimmers miss it
The polite, formal tone makes the request feel optional to readers
The subject line 'Update' gives no cue that action is required

items.prompt: A manager emails her team: 'Please update the tracker and send the figures to Priya, Marcus and Lena before the review.' Two staff each send figures to all three people, and nobody updates the tracker. Which analysis best explains what went wrong?

options.label: The sentence has too many names, so readers confuse recipients with the people responsible for the work
The sentence names no owner for each task, so each reader can assume the other task is someone else's
The sentence lacks a greeting, so readers do not register that the email was addressed to them personally
The sentence is a polite request, so readers treat it as a suggestion that can be skipped before the review

rubric: Two tasks with no assigned owner produce duplicated and missed work.
Other options attribute the failure to names, politeness or greeting rather than missing assignment.

items.prompt: You must tell a client their delivery will slip two weeks. Criteria: preserve trust, give the new date, avoid blaming others, stay under 100 words. Which opening best meets them?

options.label: 'Due to supplier failures outside our control, your order cannot ship on time, and we hope you will understand.'
'There may be some changes to the original schedule, so please check back with us soon for further details.'
'We are very sorry to inform you of an unfortunate delay, and we deeply regret any inconvenience that this may cause.'
'Your order will now ship on 14 June, two weeks later than planned; here is what we are doing to hold that date.'

rubric: It states the new date plainly, owns the delay and promises action without blame.
The blaming, over-apologetic and vague options each break a stated criterion.

items.prompt: A forecast paragraph must be cut by a third. Criterion: keep the caveat that the forecast assumes no price change, since omitting it could mislead. Which revision is best?

options.label: 'Sales should rise about 8% next year, assuming no price change.'
'Sales should rise about 8% next year, which is a strong and encouraging result.'
'Sales should rise about 8% next year, a figure based on our internal model.'
'Sales should rise about 8% next year, and the team has full confidence in this.'

rubric: It cuts length while retaining the essential assumption.
Distractors keep the length down but drop the caveat, replacing it with praise, confidence or method.

items.prompt: A reorganisation changes roles for 40 staff. Criteria: accurate, limits rumours, sensitive to individuals, leaves a record. Which plan best meets them?

options.label: Let each manager explain the changes verbally in their own way, so messages can be tailored to each team
Hold a short live briefing for the group, then send a written summary the same day with a contact for questions
Send one company-wide email at 5 pm so everyone receives identical wording at exactly the same time
Post the details on the intranet and let staff find them, since this creates a permanent record for all

rubric: A live briefing handles sensitivity and questions, and the same-day written follow-up gives a record and consistency.
Email-only, ad hoc verbal and passive intranet options each fail at least two criteria.

items.prompt: A director has two minutes to decide. A writer proposes an executive summary opening with five paragraphs of caveats, then the recommendation. Which critique is best?

options.label: The summary should be longer, because two minutes is enough to read the caveats if they are well organised and clearly headed
The caveats are right to lead, because a reader should know the main limitations before judging a recommendation at all
The summary should open with the recommendation and key figure, then the one risk that could change the decision
The summary should drop the caveats from the opening, because mentioning risk up front makes a recommendation look weak

rubric: Time-limited decision makers need the recommendation first plus only the decisive risk, with detail below.
Distractors either bury the ask, ignore the time limit or hide material risk.

items.prompt: A 30-page report with no summary is sent to a board that meets tomorrow. Rank the risks. Which is the most serious?

options.label: The board may not find the decision it must make, so tomorrow's meeting proceeds without informed input
The report may take the writer longer to produce than a shorter version would have taken
The report may contain a few minor formatting inconsistencies that could slightly lower its polish
The cover email may be slightly more formal than the board's usual style of correspondence

rubric: The main risk is that readers cannot locate the decision or conclusion in time to act on it.
The other options are cosmetic or concern writer effort rather than reader outcome.

items.prompt: A customer is angry about a billing error. Criteria: acknowledge the problem, give a specific next step, avoid admitting legal liability. Which sentences fit the reply? Select all that apply.

options.label: 'You will receive a corrected statement by Friday.'
'We take billing accuracy seriously, and we value you as a customer.'
'This was entirely our fault and we will compensate you for all losses.'
'I can see the charge appears twice, and I am reviewing it now.'

rubric: The first two acknowledge the issue and commit to a concrete step without conceding liability.
One option admits liability; the other is generic and offers no next step.

items.prompt: You are asking a CFO to approve a 50,000 software purchase. She reads only the first page and decides by Friday. Criteria: the decision must be clear, the cost-benefit visible, and risks honest. Which one-page structure is best?

options.label: Company background, vendor history, feature list, then the cost on the final line of the page
Executive enthusiasm and customer quotes first, then a summary of cost and a request for approval last
Detailed risk analysis first, then cost, then recommendation, so the CFO sees every danger before the ask
Recommendation and cost up front, then savings against cost, the main risk, and the date a decision is needed

rubric: Leading with the ask, cost-benefit, risk and deadline suits a time-limited decision maker.
Other structures bury the decision or the cost, or lead with material the CFO did not request.

items.prompt: You must email a VP for a budget decision by Friday. She reads on her phone between meetings and acts only on messages where the ask is unmistakable. Which opening best meets these criteria?

options.label: Quick question about budgets when you have a moment; happy to walk through the whole history if that is useful.
I hope your week is going well. I wanted to share some background on the vendor evaluation we have been running.
Decision needed by Friday: approve $40k for vendor B or we lose the March slot. Details below.
Following several discussions with the team, we have compiled the attached analysis of three vendors for your review.

rubric: The key puts the ask, deadline and consequence in the first line, which suits a skimming mobile reader.
The distractors open with pleasantries, vague questions or background, so the ask stays hidden.

items.prompt: A colleague says: 'In any bad-news message, cushion with context first and state the decision last.' In which situation does this advice most clearly break down?

options.label: Telling a candidate they were not selected after a final-round interview that took place last week
Telling a supplier to stop shipping a defective part today, when any delay in the key fact risks harm
Declining a long-standing client's request for a discount that they have already asked for twice this year
Informing staff that the annual bonus will be smaller because of a weak quarter in the retail division

rubric: When the reader must act immediately to prevent harm, the key fact must lead; cushioning wastes critical time.
The other cases are ordinary bad news where tone and sequencing are a matter of judgement, not urgency.

items.prompt: A client was invoiced twice by mistake. Criteria for the reply: acknowledge the error plainly, state the fix and when it took effect, avoid defensiveness, avoid over-emoting. Which reply best meets them?

options.label: We are so incredibly sorry and deeply ashamed about the horrible mistake; please forgive us for this terrible invoice problem.
As per our terms, invoices may be reissued; you were billed twice, and the matter is being reviewed by our finance team.
Unfortunately a system glitch caused a duplicate invoice, which can happen; we trust you understand and appreciate your patience.
We invoiced you twice in error. The duplicate is reversed, and your account shows the credit as of today.

rubric: The key owns the error, gives the fix and timing, and stays measured.
Distractors deflect blame, over-apologise, or hide behind terms and an open-ended review.

items.prompt: A proposal goes to a sceptical CFO who will read only the executive summary before deciding whether to read further. Judged by the risk of losing her support, which flaw in the draft is most damaging?

options.label: Two date formats appear in the timeline table, which makes some milestones look inconsistent to careful readers
The word 'utilise' is used three times where 'use' would be plainer, which slightly raises the reading level
The summary lists features but buries the total cost and payback period on page nine, where the CFO may never look
Headings mix title case and sentence case, so the document looks less polished than the firm's other proposals

rubric: Missing the figures this reader needs in the section she reads undermines the decision itself.
The others are real but cosmetic and would not by themselves lose the decision.

items.prompt: A report must recommend dropping a project that the review committee strongly favours. The committee is technical, will scrutinise the evidence, and must decide at one meeting. Which structure best meets these criteria?

options.label: Open by praising the committee's current approach at length, then give the recommendation in a single closing sentence on page six
Lead with the recommendation and leave out the counter-evidence to keep it short, since the appendix covers the detail
Walk through the investigation chronologically so the conclusion feels earned, and state the recommendation in the final paragraph
Lead with the recommendation, then give evidence strongest first, and answer the committee's most likely objection directly

rubric: A scrutinising reader with one meeting needs the conclusion up front plus visible, honest handling of objections.
Chronology and delayed conclusions waste scarce time; omitting counter-evidence destroys credibility.

items.prompt: A draft memo to 200 staff announces a new expense policy effective 1 July. It gives four paragraphs of background, states the rule in paragraph four ('employees should endeavour to keep claims reasonable') and attaches the 12-page policy. The goal is compliance by skimming readers. Which criticisms are valid? Select all that apply.

options.label: The rule and its effective date should lead, since most readers will not reach paragraph four.
Attaching the full policy is a mistake, because staff should never receive supporting documents with a memo.
'Should endeavour to keep claims reasonable' is too vague to enforce; it needs a specific limit and 'must'.
A memo is the wrong format, because policy changes may only be communicated verbally.

rubric: Valid criticisms are the buried action and the vague, unenforceable wording.
Attachments for reference are normal practice, and memos are a standard policy channel.

items.prompt: A manager must brief a director who was not on a 14-message email thread. The director must choose between two suppliers tomorrow and has ten minutes today. The thread contains the facts but also tangents and a disagreement. Which approach best serves the director?

options.label: Write a fresh note stating the decision, the two options with costs, and your recommendation, linking the thread.
Reply to the thread adding the director in copy and asking her to scroll up and choose one of the options.
Summarise all 14 messages in time order so the director sees how each view developed before the decision.
Forward the full thread to the director with 'see below' so nothing is filtered and she can judge for herself.

rubric: A purpose-built note puts the decision and trade-offs in front of a time-pressed reader, with the thread as backup.
The others push the synthesis work onto the director or bury the decision in history.

items.prompt: You must write a subject line for an email to six teams about a Saturday 02:00-04:00 system outage. Constraints: under 60 characters, states the required action and its deadline (save work by Friday 18:00), and is easy to find in a later inbox search. Which line meets all of them?

options.label: Important update regarding upcoming system maintenance activities this weekend
Saturday outage 02:00-04:00 – please read the full message for details on timing
IT notice: scheduled work – no action needed unless you see problems later
Action by Fri 18:00: save work before Sat 02:00 outage

rubric: Only the key is under 60 characters and gives both the action and the deadline plus searchable terms.
Distractors are vague, too long, or wrongly say no action is needed.

items.prompt: Design a memo for these constraints: the body must fit one page, the executives who decide will read only that page, two analysts need the method details, and a decision is needed within a week. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Write two separate memos with different recommendations so each audience gets text tailored to it, and let the executives choose.
Put the full method and data tables on page one so the analysts are satisfied, and summarise the decision in a footnote.
Give a chronological account of the analysis on page one and place the recommendation in the closing paragraph of page two.
Open page one with the recommendation, decision date and cost, then give key reasons, and put method details in a referenced appendix.

rubric: The key serves decision-makers on one page and still gives analysts a place for method.
Distractors break the page limit, bury the decision, or split the recommendation.

items.prompt: You must plan a proposal that both a CFO (cost and return) and a lead engineer (technical feasibility) must approve. Each reads only the parts relevant to them, and both sign off in the same meeting. Which plan meets these constraints?

options.label: Open with a summary of the request, cost and return, then add labelled finance and engineering sections that each lead with a conclusion.
Write the technical design in full first, since feasibility must be settled before money matters, and attach the financials last as an appendix.
Write one continuous narrative that blends cost and technical points so both readers must read every section to follow the argument.
Write two separate proposals for different readers, each with its own recommendation, and ask them to reconcile the differences in the meeting.

rubric: The key gives a shared decision request plus modular sections that let each reader find what matters.
Distractors force full reading, ignore the CFO's needs, or split the recommendation.

items.prompt: A team proposes this template for incident emails to customers: headline, what happened, who is affected, apology. The constraint is that readers must know what to do and when to expect news. What does the template lack?

options.label: A longer apology signed by the CEO to show the issue is taken seriously at the top
The action customers must take, if any, and the time of the next update
A detailed technical root-cause timeline that lets customers verify the engineering response themselves
The names and roles of every engineer involved so customers know who is working on it

rubric: The template gives no next step and no expectation for follow-up, which the constraint requires.
The distractors add detail or tone that does not help readers act or plan.

items.prompt: A project email copied to five people got no replies. It opens with two paragraphs of context; the request for three people to confirm their deliverables is in the last line, with no names or dates. Which revision best fixes the causes?

options.label: Forward the email to the recipients' managers noting that the team has not replied, to prompt a response.
Resend the same text with URGENT in the subject so the request stands out from other messages in the inbox.
Add a longer introduction explaining why the project matters so recipients feel motivated to respond promptly.
Name each person's single task and due date on separate lines, with the ask in the first sentence.

rubric: The silence stems from a buried ask and no ownership; naming tasks and dates fixes both.
The distractors add pressure or length without changing structure or accountability.

items.prompt: You are rewriting a letter that declines a customer's refund request outside the 30-day window. Constraints: state the decision clearly, preserve the relationship, and give the customer a next step. Which elements must the rewrite include? Select all that apply.

options.label: A repair or credit option the customer can still use, with how to claim it
The full legal clause quoted in its entirety so the refusal cannot be argued with
A plain statement of the decision with the one policy reason that applies, without blame
Repeated apologies in each paragraph in place of stating the policy reason

rubric: The rewrite needs a clear decision with a brief reason and a usable alternative.
Over-apologising obscures the decision; quoting legal text damages the relationship.

items.prompt: A company is changing its remote-work policy. Staff need to know what changes and when, managers need to know how to handle exceptions, and customers need to know whether service hours change. Everyone must see consistent facts, and the HR team can maintain only one detailed source. Which communication plan meets all these constraints?

options.label: Let each manager explain the change in their own words, since local framing will help staff accept the change.
Send the full policy text to every audience in the same email so that nobody receives a different version of events.
Publish one master announcement, then send short audience notes that lead with each group's action and link to it.
Write three independent notes with no shared master so each audience gets fully tailored detail and no extra text.

rubric: A single master source plus short audience-specific notes keeps facts consistent while serving each reader's needs.
Identical mass text ignores audience needs; manager paraphrase and independent notes risk inconsistent facts and multiple sources.
